1:
The dialogue turns here to its most searching meditation on human frailty, and the witnesses gather around the opening portrait of a creature "born of a woman," "of few days, and full of trouble." The reformed John Gill takes the description of earthly man, every descendant of Adam, yet holds that Job "chiefly designs himself": having spoken of his wasting circumstances in the previous chapter, he now treats of his frailty and mortality, and improves it into an argument with God for pity and mercy. Gill hears a possible glance back at Eve, the mother of all living, from whom every man is born.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the verse as a doctrine of the original, the frailty, and the pollution of human life. Man is "born of a woman," which may point to Eve, called the mother of all living, who being deceived was first in the transgression, so that we derive from her the sin and corruption that both shorten and sadden our days; or to every man's immediate mother, the weaker vessel, for partus sequitur ventrem, the child takes after the mother. Let not the strong man glory in his strength, Henry warns, but remember that when God pleases the mighty become as women, as in Jer. 51:30. The nature of that life is a fading flower and a fleeting shadow, computed not by years but by days, for we cannot be sure of any day but that it may be our last.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke finds a delicacy in the Hebrew — Adam yelud ishah, "Adam born of a woman, few of days, and full of tremor." The first Adam, who did not spring from woman but was formed immediately by God, lived nine hundred and thirty years; but the Adam who now springs from woman by ordinary generation has very few, seventy at the highest average, and those full of rogez, cares, anxieties, and tremors: he seems born not to live but to die, and by living forfeits his title to life. John Wesley agrees, reading man as a weak creature, corrupt and sinful, and born "of that sex by which sin and all other calamity was brought into the world." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the verse at the head of the whole complaint, where Job rises from his own particular case to the common lot of the race, picturing beforehand the miserable creature with whom God will have to contend if he contends with him at all.
2:
From the fact of frailty the witnesses move to its two great images, the flower and the shadow. The reformed John Gill draws out the likeness: as the flower comes from the earth and the man from his mother's womb, so both flourish a while and then fade. He reads Job's own history into it — the time before his troubles, when he was the greatest man of the east, his children like olive plants about his table, himself in perfect health; a flower at full blow, yet presently decayed, "easily and quickly cut down by death, like a beautiful flower cut with the knife, or cropped by the hand, or trampled upon by the foot."

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the shadow further. The flower is a frequent figure in the writers of both Testaments; and man, "as he appears among men, is only the shadow of his real, substantial, and eternal being." Compared to a vegetable, he springs up, bears his flower, is nipped by disease and blasted by affliction, and at last is cut down by death, the bloom of youth being only the forerunner of hoary hairs, enfeebled muscles, impaired senses, and dissolution. All these images, Clarke says, are finely embodied and happily expressed, and he promises to gather them into the beautiful lines of a poet he will quote at the chapter's close. John Wesley keeps to the plain force of the two figures: the flower is fading, and all its beauty soon withers and is gone; the shadow is fleeting, and its very being will soon be lost in the shadows of night — and of neither, he adds, do we make any account or put any confidence.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the couplet in its Hebrew and press its theology of birth. Man is "short of days and full of unrest," coming forth as a flower and cut down, fleeing as a shadow that continues not; and they ground the misery in the manner of his coming, for woman is weak, brings forth in pain, and is unclean in her lying-in, so that weakness, suffering, and impurity are man's portion from the very birth — a thought they carry to the kindred sayings of ch. 15:14 and ch. 25:4. The witnesses do not divide; they converge on a single portrait of a life that blooms only to be cut, and casts only a shadow that will not stay, so that the frailty owned in the first verse is now made visible in the fastest-fading things the eye can name.
3:
The frail creature just described becomes, in this verse, the object of a scrutiny Job feels as menace: "dost thou open thine eyes upon such an one, and bringest me into judgment with thee?" The reformed John Gill is careful to say what the opened eyes are not. They are not the providential care whose eyes run to and fro throughout the earth, nor the eyes of love, grace, and mercy that God opens upon his own peculiar people and never withdraws; they are, as Job took his own case to be, the exercise of rigorous justice in punishing and chastising with severity. God's eyes, he thought, were set on him for evil and not for good; he "looked wistly on him, and in a very frowning manner," sharpened his eye upon him, looked narrowly into all his ways, watched every motion and every step he took, and pursued him with great eagerness and strictness.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the second clause Job's plea against such strict cognizance. "Since I have such a corrupt nature within, and am liable to so much trouble," he paraphrases, "dost thou open thine eyes and fasten them upon such a one, extremely to mark what I do amiss? and dost thou bring me, such a worthless worm as I am, into judgment with thee" — with a God so quick-sighted to discover the least failing, so holy to hate it, so just to condemn, and so mighty to punish? The consideration of our own inability to contend with God, Henry urges, and of our own sinfulness and weakness, should engage us rather to pray, "Lord, enter not into judgment with thy servant."

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lifts the eye from the particular grievance to the shape of the whole chapter, observing that from this point "the whole of this chapter is directed to God alone; in no part of it does he take any notice of his friends." The debate that had run through the earlier speeches is for the moment suspended; Job turns from Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar and speaks only upward. The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as the cry of a man who feels the divine gaze not as protection but as prosecution, and who marvels that so great and holy a God should stoop to arraign so brief and broken a thing as man — the very disproportion Job means to press as a reason for mercy rather than judgment.
4:
Job grounds his appeal for leniency in the taint he was born with — "who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one." The reformed John Gill reads it as the impossibility of producing a clean person from an unclean one: the first man, though made upright, defiled himself and all human nature in him, so that all who descend from him by ordinary generation are conceived and shaped in iniquity, and it is not possible that man born of a woman should be free from sin. The sinfulness of human nature, Gill concludes, is thus unavoidable and natural, and "there is none righteous or pure from sin."

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke refers the verse to man's original and corrupt nature: every man comes into the world in a sinful state, derived from fallen Adam to the utmost ramifications of the human family, and from this corruption of nature God alone can save. He gathers the old versions around it — the Chaldee, "Who will produce a clean thing from man, who is polluted with sins, except God, who is one?"; Coverdale's blunt "Who can make it cleane, that commeth of an uncleane thinge? No body"; and the Alexandrian Greek, "Who is pure from corruption? Not one, although he had lived but one day upon the earth." John Wesley reads the closing "not one" as "no man," and hears in the verse a prayer: cleansing "is the prerogative of thy grace, which therefore I humbly implore."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes the question as the lament of a sanctified man tracing the streams up to their fountain: actual transgressions are the natural product of habitual corruption, which is therefore called original sin because it is the original of all our sins. He too hears it pleaded for compassion — "Lord, be not extreme to mark my sins of human frailty, for thou knowest my weakness; O remember that I am flesh" — and notes the Chaldee's reading, that God, who is one, can by his almighty grace change even the skin of the Ethiopian. Here the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott raises a genuine alternative. The received sense makes the verse a flat statement of universal impurity, reiterated by Bildad at ch. 25:4; but Ellicott suggests it may rather be rendered as a wish — "Oh, that the clean could come forth from the unclean! but none can." So the witnesses agree on the doctrine of inborn defilement, and differ only on the grammar: whether Job states that no clean thing can come from an unclean, or sighs that it cannot.
5:
The appointed limit of human life draws the witnesses, and here a patristic voice joins them. The latin-fathers Gregory the Great makes the shortness of life a discipline of the righteous, who "think of the present life, how transitory it is," the more heedfully as they take thought of the eternal blessings of the heavenly country. On the words "the number of his months is with thee," Gregory finds a comfort hidden in the very brevity: what runs by so rapidly seems not to be with us at all, yet since even things passing away stand fast with Almighty God, the days that are short to us are, in their multiplied months, "recorded to be with God"; and the clause "thou hast appointed his bounds" he refers to that secret counsel by which God, foreseeing all things, decreed before the ages how they should be ordered.

The reformed John Gill glosses "his days are determined" as "cut out," exactly and precisely, how many a man shall live and what shall befall him every day; and because life is so short, it is reckoned rather by days than by years. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke enlarges the thought to the whole race: the general term of human life is fixed by God, and in vain are all attempts to prolong it. He runs through the seekers of an elixir — Paracelsus, Van Helmont, Artephius, and the rest — who promised endless repair of the body and are themselves long dead; and though God may here and there produce a Thomas Parr or a Henry Jenkins who lived beyond a century and a half, these rare instances do not affect the general term, for "dust thou art, and unto dust thou shalt return" renders every such pretension nugatory. Yet the bounds, Clarke insists, apply to the race and not to the individual, for folly and intemperance abridge many a life short of them.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse and its neighbours together and turn at once to the great contrast the passage is building: the determined days, the numbered months, the fixed bound man cannot pass, all set the stage for the tree that may sprout again where man cannot. Job, they say, "a true child of his age, has a still sadder conception of the destiny of man in death," and the conflict he is passing through makes that conception sadder still. The witnesses do not contend; they read one settled truth — that the span of every life is measured out by God — but they weigh it differently, Gregory and Gill finding in it the hand of a God who remembers, while Keil and Delitzsch already hear the sadness that will darken the verses to come.
6:
Having owned the fixed bound of life, Job asks for a little ease within it: "turn from him, that he may rest, till he shall accomplish, as an hireling, his day." The reformed John Gill weighs what the turning means. It is not that Job wishes God to withdraw his gracious or supporting presence, than which nothing is more agreeable to a good man; it is a plea that God would turn away from afflicting him in this extraordinary manner, taking off the hand that pressed him so sorely, since in the ordinary course of things he had troubles enough and but a little time to live. He notes a harsher construction some prefer — "turn from him, that he may cease," a wish for death and its rest in the grave — but inclines to the gentler sense of a respite short of dying.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it in the same key, taking the image of the hireling to its natural close: cease to try him by afflictions, that he may enjoy some of the comforts of life before he is removed from it; and as a labourer is permitted by his master to take a little repose in the heat of the day, so Job asks a breathing-time from affliction before he comes to that bound he cannot pass — a request he had made before, at ch. 10:20. John Wesley glosses it briefly to the same effect: "withdraw thine afflicting hand from him, that he may have some present ease," till he come to the period of his life which God has allotted him, as a man appoints a set time to a hired servant.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses a nicety in the last word. "Accomplish," he says, is rather "have pleasure in" — that the hireling might "rejoice at the day when his wages are paid him," a turn Job had used already at ch. 7:2. Ellicott then marks the movement of the argument, for Job now proceeds to enlarge on the mortality of man, comparing him, as is so often done in all literature, to the vegetable produce of the earth — with this difference, that a tree will sprout again when it is cut down, but even a strong man succumbs to death, "yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he?" The witnesses converge on a plea for mercy's respite, and differ only over that single verb — whether the labourer merely finishes his day, or is granted to take some pleasure in it before the wages of death are paid.
7:
"For there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again" — the great image at the chapter's heart, over which the witnesses begin to divide on the darkest question of the book. The reformed John Gill explains the botany: if a tree be felled to the root, and only the stump left in the ground, its owner may yet hope it is not utterly destroyed but will bud out again, renewing its strength and putting forth new shoots, as the laurel or the willow. Not every tree does so — the cypress, once cut down, sprouts no more — but enough do to serve Job's purpose, which is to set the tree's hope against man's hopelessness.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the contrast at its bleakest. "As the tree falleth so it lieth, says a cheerless proverb," they observe; but Job, "a true child of his age, has a still sadder conception of the destiny of man in death," and the conflict he endures makes it sadder yet. The fate of the tree is far from so hopeless as man's, for the hewn tree sprouts, and at the mere scent of water buds like a young plant, while man, once fallen, is "gone without leaving a trace of life." For Keil and Delitzsch the whole passage measures how much less favoured man is than the felled tree.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, in a long exposition of these verses, hears the same contrast but carries it past despair. Death, he grants, is a removal for ever out of this world: a man cut down will not revive as a tree does, for the vegetable life is a cheap and easy thing that the scent of water recovers, but the rational soul, once retired, is too noble a thing to be recalled by any power of nature, and can be restored only "by the immediate operations of Omnipotence itself." Yet that Omnipotence, Henry insists, will act; there will be a return of man to life in another world at the end of time, when the heavens are no more, for "the resurrection of the dead was doubtless an article of Job's creed," as appears at ch. 19:26, and to that he has an eye even here. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the natural history from Calmet: not every old and rotted stem, but many trees grown from cuttings, or dried by long exposure, will on being replanted take root and resume their verdure, and few there are that will not send forth new shoots when cut level with the earth. So the witnesses share the image and part on its reach — Keil and Delitzsch finding in the sprouting tree only the foil to man's ruin, Henry and Clarke already looking past the felled stump to a resurrection the tree can but faintly shadow.
8:
The tree's resilience is pressed to its extreme, so that even age and apparent death cannot cancel its hope. The reformed John Gill takes "though the root thereof wax old in the earth" as the case least likely to revive: the root lies long in the ground, grown dry and seemingly consumed, so that there might well be the less hope of its flourishing — and yet, as the next verse will say, it does. The whole force of the couplet is to grant the tree every disadvantage and still leave it its future.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the two verses as one movement toward the crushing "how much less" that follows. Though the root grow old and the stock die off in the dust, yet at the scent of water it buds and brings forth boughs like a young plant; and against that they set the fate of man, who "dieth and wasteth away," lies "there completely broken down and melted away," and once fallen together "is gone without leaving a trace of life." The tree's death is a sleep from which water wakes it; man's is a dissolution from which nothing wakes him in this world. John Wesley adds only the pointed qualification that fixes the whole comparison: the stock and root "die," he says, but only "to outward appearance" — the seeming death of the tree being precisely what makes its revival so apt a foil to the real and final death of man.

The wesleyan-arminian and reformed witnesses do not divide over the sense; the verse is a single sustained concession, heaping up the tree's disadvantages — an aged root, a dead stock, the dust closing over both — only to overturn them. Gill dwells on that seeming hopelessness, the root grown dry and to all appearance consumed, precisely so that its revival may be the more surprising; and Keil and Delitzsch let the same picture stand as the dark ground against which man's ruin is measured. What they are together building is the ground of Job's complaint, that the meanest vegetable enjoys a resurrection denied to the noblest of God's earthly creatures. The reader is meant to feel the injustice of it as Job felt it: that a felled willow should have more prospect of another spring than a buried man has of another life, so that the very kindness of nature to the tree throws the hardness of man's lot into sharper relief. The strength of the image lies in its patience, granting the tree its long burial in order to make its budding the more wonderful — and man's silence in the grave the more bitter.
9:
The turn the whole comparison has been waiting for arrives with the budding of the tree: "yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant." The reformed John Gill lingers on the vividness of the phrase "the scent of water" — as soon as the tree smells it, perceives it, or partakes of its efficacy, it buds; the words denote both how speedily and how easily, at once as it were, revival comes through the virtue of rain that descends upon it or river-water by which it is planted. He instances the willow above all, which delights in watery places and will, by the mere benefit of water, bud out again even when its stock had seemed dead.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke prizes the metaphor for its delicacy, calling it "a fine metaphor": the water acts upon the decaying and perishing tree "as strong and powerful odours from musk, otto of roses, ammonia, and the like, act on a fainting or swooning person." The dying tree is like one in a swoon, and the scent of water is the reviving draught held to its senses; a touch of moisture recalls it as a strong perfume recalls the faint. John Wesley keeps close to the words, noting that "scent" means simply "by means of water," and that scent or smell is here figuratively ascribed to a tree — the poet lending the senseless stump a power of perception, so that it seems to catch the nearness of water and stir toward it.

The witnesses do not divide; they dwell together on the tenderness and speed of the tree's recovery precisely because it measures, by contrast, the finality of man's death in the verses that follow. Gill notes how the willow, of all trees, thrives beside the water and will bud from a stock that seemed dead; Clarke likens the reviving to a swooning person recalled by a strong scent; Wesley marks the poetic fiction that lends the stump a power of perception. Everything that makes the budding lovely — its quickness, its ease, its response to so slight a thing as the smell of water — is what Job cannot claim for himself. The stump feels the water and lives; the buried man feels nothing and does not. So the very charm of the image carries its sting, and the witnesses let the reader admire the reviving tree only to feel, a verse later, how much poorer is the lot of the man who has no such spring to look for, and whom no scent of water will ever wake.
10:
"But man dieth, and wasteth away: yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he?" — the hinge on which the comparison swings from the tree's hope to man's despair. The reformed John Gill lets the verse gather in all sorts and conditions: the mighty man dies in his full strength, the wise man for all his skill in medicine, the rich man whom no riches can bribe death away, the great and honourable whose honour is laid in the dust, and even good men for whom Christ has died; all have sinned, and death passes upon all. Death, he says, is the separation of soul and body, and when it is made the body "wasteth away" in the grave.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the two names the verse uses for man. It is Geber, the mighty man, who "though mighty, dies," and Adam, the man of earth, who "because earthy, gives up the ghost." Henry traces the stages: before death man wastes away, dying daily, spending upon the quick stock of life; in death he gives up the ghost, the soul leaving the body and returning to God the Father of spirits; and after death comes the awful question, "where is he?" He is not where he was, his place knows him no more — yet not nowhere, for he is gone to the world of spirits, gone into eternity, gone to return no more to this world. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the Hebrew to the same cheerless effect: the man who has once fallen together lies "there stretched out," broken down and melted away, and is gone without leaving a trace of life.

The wesleyan-arminian voices press the pathos of that closing "where is he?" John Wesley distinguishes the mighty Geber who yet dies from the earthy Adam who returns to his dust, and answers the question with a solemn certainty: not where he was, his place knows him no more, "but is he nowhere? Yes, he is gone to the world of spirits, gone into eternity, gone never to return to this world." Adam Clarke hears the same note echoed in the poets, quoting the Persian Khosroo, who wandered among the tombs asking "Where are they?" and heard only Fate give back by Echo the answer, "Where are they?" The witnesses do not divide over the fact of death's finality in this world; but already they lean, some toward the silence of the grave and some toward the world of spirits beyond it, opening the very question the next verses will strain against.
11:
Job reaches for a second figure, the drying up of waters, and the witnesses split over just how much despair it carries. The reformed John Gill notes that the line may be read without the "as," as a plain dissimilitude: the waters go from the sea and return again with the tide, but man does not return. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes it of evaporation — the waters drawn up from the sea, the river partly dried and absorbed crossing the desert, yet the sea not exhausted, for the vapours condense and fall as rain and by rivers return again; "so man is imperceptibly removed from his fellows by death, yet the human race is still continued" by perpetual generations. John Wesley reads the comparison the other way, of a sea that forsakes its place so that the river it fed "decayeth and drieth up without all hopes of recovery."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses hardest on the grammar and finds in it a whole theology. There is no particle of comparison in the Hebrew, he insists, and the sea does not in fact fail, nor do the Nile and Euphrates dry up; the implied likeness is one of contrariety — "the waters will have failed from the sea, and the rivers will have wasted and become dry, and yet the man who hath lain down in death will not arise," that is, sooner than man rises the sea itself will fail. And here Ellicott weighs the resurrection question with unusual care: "there is no hope of any future life, still less of any resurrection here; but neither can we regard the language as involving an absolute denial of it." What Job says holds true even in full view of the life to come; indeed, "there seems to glimmer the hope of an ardent though unexpressed longing, through the very language that is used," a hope not proof against the doubt that will break out in the next verse.

Keil and Delitzsch keep the sterner reading, taking the running and drying water as the very figure of a vanishing "without hope and beyond recovery." So the witnesses genuinely divide: Clarke finds in the water-cycle an image of the race renewed even as the man departs; Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch hear only irrecoverable loss; and Ellicott holds the two in tension, refusing both a confident resurrection and a flat denial, and catching beneath Job's bleakest words the flicker of a longing he cannot yet name.
12:
The two figures come to rest in a flat declaration of the grave's permanence: "so man lieth down, and riseth not: till the heavens be no more, they shall not awake." The reformed John Gill reads the lying-down gently, as of one who takes his rest: man lies down in the grave when he dies, as on a bed, and takes his rest from all his labours, toil, and troubles, and continues asleep "till the resurrection morn." The clause that seems to shut the door — "till the heavens be no more" — Gill hears as marking the term of the sleep, not its endlessness; the dead lie until that last dissolution of the visible heavens, and no longer.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the verse into a defence of the resurrection against those who would make it a denial. Men shall not, like felled trees and cut plants, reproduce their like, nor rise "till the heavens are no more, till the earth and all its works are burnt up, and the general resurrection of human beings shall take place"; but "surely it would be difficult to twist this passage to the denial of the resurrection of the body," nor can the words be fairly understood to teach that the soul is material or sleeps entire until that day. Job, Clarke reminds his reader, elsewhere distinguishes the animal life from the rational soul, and "the doctrine of the materiality of the soul, and its sleep till the resurrection, has no place in the sacred records." He calls the contrary reading "a cold and comfortless philosophy," and points forward to the next verse as proof that Job did not hold it. John Wesley reads the terms plainly: man lieth down "in his bed, the grave," and rises not "till the time of the general resurrection, when these visible heavens shall pass away."

The witnesses here do not divide but reinforce one another against a misreading. What the verse denies, they agree, is any return to this present life and world — man does not, like the tree, sprout again into the old existence — not the resurrection at the last day, which the very phrase "till the heavens be no more" leaves standing beyond the long night of the grave. Job's despair, on their reading, is a despair of this world only; and the tender image of lying down to sleep, which Gill and Wesley both keep, already holds within it the promise of a morning, however distant, when the sleepers shall be raised.
13:
From despair Job turns to petition, longing to be hidden in the grave until the storm of wrath is overpast: "O that thou wouldest hide me in the grave... until thy wrath be past, that thou wouldest appoint me a set time, and remember me." The reformed John Gill reads the wish first as a craving for shelter from present misery — the grave as "the house appointed for all living," where the dead lie insensible of the calamities of this world, or some subterraneous place where Job might be buried alive rather than remain above ground with his sorrows. The stress for Gill falls on escape from suffering, the grave as a hiding-place from the indignation abroad in the world.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws the verse into a full confession of resurrection hope, and carefully distinguishes its clauses. "Hide me in the grave" concerns the body; "keep me secret" concerns the spirit, hidden with God where no enemy can invade its repose. But the decisive words are "appoint me a set time, and remember me": having spoken of the body's death and the spirit's secreting, Job "must refer here to the resurrection," for what else could a man desire whose body is mingled with the dust? When the debt of death is paid and "thy wrath, thy displeasure, against the body is past," then, Clarke has Job pray, "remember me — raise my body, unite my spirit to it, and receive both into thy glory for ever." John Wesley reads it the same way: the grave is "not only a resting-place, but a hiding-place to the children of God," who hides them there as a man hides his treasure in safety, "not only from the storms of this life, but for the glory of a better"; and the "set time" is the appointed day of their being remembered, as Noah was remembered in the ark at Gen. 8:1.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the verse a humble petition for a hiding-place, offered "not only in a passionate weariness of this life, but in a pious assurance of a better." God has the key of the grave, to let in now and to let out at the resurrection; he hides his people there as we hide our treasure, and "he who hides will find, and nothing shall be lost." The saints lie until God's wrath be wholly past — which it will be when the body is raised and death, the last enemy, destroyed — and until the set time comes for their being remembered. So a real difference of emphasis surfaces: Gill hears chiefly a longing to be sheltered from misery, while Clarke, Wesley, and Henry hear a deliberate reach toward the resurrection, the grave itself made a reserved chamber against the day God shall remember his own.
14:
"If a man die, shall he live again?" — the question the whole chapter has been circling, and the witnesses divide over both its tone and the "change" for which Job resolves to wait. The reformed John Gill takes the opening not as real doubt but as settled certainty of death, which the experience of all men confirms, though he notes the Targum restrains the whole to the wicked. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the surrounding verses at their darkest, hearing Job say that God has sealed up his transgression and destroyed the hope of man; for them the question hangs unanswered over a bleak scene.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, by contrast, finds here "a strong persuasion of the certainty of the general resurrection." "All the days of my appointed time," he shows, is literally "of my warfare," the term Job had used at ch. 7:1; and "till my change come" is till my renovation come, the word used for the springing again of grass in Ps. 90:5-6 after it has withered — "in itself a very expressive emblem of the resurrection." Job, on this reading, waits out his whole warfare in the hope of rising renewed like grass after winter. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry holds two readings open. Taken of the resurrection, when the vile body shall be changed as in Phil. 3:21, the question becomes a cry of wonder — "Shall these dry bones live? If so, my separate soul shall wait until that change comes, when it shall be reunited to the body, and my flesh also shall rest in hope." Taken of the change at death, it means rather, "No, not such a life as I now live; and therefore I will patiently wait until that change comes which will put a period to my calamities."

That second sense is exactly where John Wesley lands: "shall he live? — he shall not in this world; therefore I will patiently wait till that change comes, which will put a period to my calamities." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, however, will not let the question be read as flat denial: "Why ask the question," he presses, "if it were absolutely certain that he would not?" He paraphrases the whole — "as long as I live I will hope, till my change from life to death comes, that thou shalt call and I shall answer thee, that thou wilt long for the work of thine hands." So the witnesses circle the deepest crux of the book without wholly resolving it: whether the "change" Job waits for is the resurrection that will reclothe his flesh, as Clarke and one side of Henry hold, or merely the change at death that ends his griefs, as Wesley and the other side of Henry take it — with Ellicott insisting that the very asking of the question betrays a hope its speaker dares not yet affirm.
15:
"Thou shalt call, and I will answer thee: thou wilt have a desire to the work of thine hands" — Job's hope rises to a scene of reunion, and the witnesses read the call at two moments. The reformed John Gill offers both. It may be the call at death, when the soul is summoned out of time into eternity and a good man, prepared for it, answers readily and cheerfully, death being to him no king of terrors; or it may be the call at the resurrection, when Christ shall cry to the dead as he cried to Lazarus, "Come forth," and they shall hear the voice of the archangel and answer, the grave being obliged to deliver up the dead that are in it.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes it firmly at the resurrection, and hears in it a divine yearning. "Thou shalt call" — "Awake, ye dead, and come to judgment"; "and I will answer thee" — "my dissolved frame shall be united at thy call, and body and soul shall be rejoined." The clause "thou wilt have a desire to the work of thine hands" he renders "thou wilt pant with desire," or "yearn over the work of thy hands": man being one of the noblest works of God, a masterpiece of his creative skill, nothing less than the strongest call upon justice could have induced God to destroy him, so that "even God is represented as earnestly longing for the ultimate reviviscence of the sleeping dust — he cannot, he will not, forget the work of his hands." John Wesley reads the same tenderness more inwardly: "thou shalt call my soul to thyself, and I will cheerfully answer, Here I am," knowing that God "wilt have a desire to the work of thy hands," a love for the soul that he has made and "new-made by thy grace."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers these into a single comfort against Job's present darkness. Now he was under such a cloud that he durst not answer God at all; but he cheers himself that a time will come when God will call and he shall answer — at the resurrection, "Thou shalt call me out of the grave by the voice of the archangel, and I will answer and come at the call"; or at death, "Thou shalt call my soul to thyself, and I will answer, Ready, Lord — coming, here I am." For grace in the soul is the work of God's own hands, and therefore, as Ps. 138:8 promises, he will not forsake it, but will have a desire to perfect it and crown it with endless glory. The witnesses do not finally divide here; whether the call sounds at death or at the last trumpet, they agree that Job has climbed, out of the grave's silence, to the astonishing thought that the God who made him will one day long to have him back.
16:
As suddenly as the hope had risen, Job's mood darkens again, and the witnesses mark the fall. The reformed John Gill catches the reversal: Job "was in a pretty good frame of mind a little before, having in view his last change and the glorious resurrection, but on a sudden he returns to his former complaints of God," now of the rigour and strictness of his justice in numbering his steps. God, Job thought, told his wrong steps one by one, marked his every aberration, and looked so narrowly to his paths that not one false step escaped the reckoning. John Wesley reads it the same way — "thou makest a strict enquiry into all my actions" — and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears the note of a persecution so persistent that it would "wear out the strongest, even as the mountain and the rock are gradually worn away."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds the verse the ground of Job's longing to be gone: he longs for the world where God's wrath is past because now he lies under its continual tokens, "as a child under the severe discipline of the rod longs to be of age." Yet Henry weighs the complaint on both sides. Job does right to divine justice in owning that he smarts for his sins, for there was sin in all his steps; but he does wrong to divine goodness in suggesting that God is "extreme to mark what he did amiss." God does indeed see all our sins, Henry allows, and sees sin even in his own people, "but he is not severe in reckoning with us, nor is the law ever stretched against us, but we are punished less than our iniquities deserve"; the transgressions of the impenitent he seals against the day of wrath, but the sins of his people he blots out as a cloud.

Against this reading of relapse the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets a strikingly hopeful construction. The opening particle, he argues, means "although" — "although thou, by thy conduct towards me, seemest bent on my utter destruction, yet thou delightest in mercy, and I shall be saved." On Clarke's rendering the verse is not a fall back into complaint at all but a continuation of the confidence of the verses before, the numbering of steps set against the settled trust that God's last word is mercy. So the witnesses genuinely divide over the verse's temper: Gill, Henry, Wesley, and Ellicott hear Job's hope collapse back into the old grievance that God watches his every sin, while Clarke hears him hold his ground, reading even the strict accounting through the assurance that the God who marks his steps still means to save him.
17:
The image of the numbered steps hardens into one of sealed evidence: "my transgression is sealed up in a bag, and thou sewest up mine iniquity." The reformed John Gill offers two ways to take the sealing. It may mean that the transgression is hidden from Job himself — sealed up so that he cannot tell what it is for which he is so severely afflicted, entirely ignorant of the charge against him. Or it may mean that God has taken strict notice of his sins, put them as it were in a bag and set a seal upon it, that none might be lost but all be ready to be produced against him another day — an allusion, Gill thinks, to the bills of indictment kept sealed in bags against a trial.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke seizes that same legal picture and dates it to his own day. The verse alludes, he says, to the custom of collecting evidence of state transgressions, sealing them in a bag, and presenting them to the judges — and he cannot resist noting that "just at this time, July 1820, charges of state transgressions, sealed up in a Green Bag and presented to the two houses of parliament, are making a considerable noise in the land." Others, he adds, take it of money sealed up in bags, common in the East. Either way the figure carries two ideas: Job's transgressions were all numbered, not one passed by, and all sealed up, so that none of them could be lost. John Wesley reads it in the same key — the sins sealed "as writings or other choice things, that they may all be brought forth upon occasion, and not one of them forgotten," so that "thou keepest all my sins in thy memory" — but he closes with a plain caution: "herein Job speaks rashly."

The witnesses do not much divide over the imagery, only over the wound it names. To Gill's first sense the bitterness is Job's ignorance of his fault, a sealed indictment he is never allowed to read; to his second, and to Clarke and Wesley, the bitterness is God's exact and unforgetting record, every sin numbered, bagged, and stitched up against the day of reckoning. And Wesley's aside sets the whole in its proper light: this is Job's grief speaking, not the sober truth of God's dealings, for the God who is charged here with hoarding every transgression is the God who elsewhere blots out the sins of his people as a cloud. The verse stands, on their reading, as the low point of Job's relapse — a good man, under the pressure of pain, imagining his God a prosecutor sewing up the evidence, when in fact mercy waits behind the seal.
18:
"And surely the mountain falling cometh to nought, and the rock is removed out of his place" — Job returns to the theme of irreparable ruin, illustrating it now from the slow decay of the strongest things in nature. The reformed John Gill unfolds the figure: a falling mountain "comes to nought," crumbling into dust where it falls and never rising to its old height; or, as the word may be rendered, it "withers," its plants and herbs dying away, or it is "dissolved," spreading itself in dust and sand never gathered up into a mountain again. So man, likened to a mountain — as kingdoms, states, and great men are — falls by death and comes to nothing, brought down and never re-advanced.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take the verse as the opening of the chapter's final and bleakest movement, gathering the falling mountain, the removed rock, the water that wears the stones, and the flood that sweeps away the dust of the earth into one crushing conclusion — "and the hope of man thou destroyest." The whole of nature's mightiest and most enduring forms are set before us only to be shown wearing away, that man's hope may be seen wearing away with them. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as a plain lesson in mutability: "everything in nature is exposed to mutability and decay — even mountains themselves may fall from their bases and be dashed to pieces, or be suddenly swallowed up by an earthquake; and by the same means the strongest and most massive rocks may be removed."

John Wesley draws the images together into a single sustained comparison, and hears in the Hebrew a particular tenderness: the great mountain, when it falls by earthquake or inundation, "moulders away like a fading leaf," as the word signifies; the rock, once thrown from its place, is never re-established; the stones are worn by the continual dropping of the waters so that they can never be made whole; and the things that grow out of the earth, once washed away by a violent flood, are irrecoverably lost. "In like manner," he concludes, "thou destroyest the hope of man: when man dies, all hope of his living again in this world is lost." The witnesses do not divide; they pile image upon image of decay precisely to make one point — that the firmest things the eye can rest on are all, in the end, worn down and swept off, and that man's hope of this life is the frailest of them all.
19:
The catalogue of decay narrows to its gentlest and most relentless instance, the wearing of stones by water. The reformed John Gill reads the figure straight into Job's own case: the waters wear the stones, whether by continual running over them or by constant dropping upon them, and the hollows they carve are never filled up again nor the stones restored to their former shape; "so man, though he may have the strength of stones, yet the waters of afflictions will gradually wear him away, and bring him to the dust of death," where he must lie till the heavens be no more. The strongest constitution, like the hardest stone, yields at last to the patient assault of trouble.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke enriches the same image with the proverb-lore of the ancients. Even the common stones are worn, he observes, and not only by earthquakes and violent concussions but by the mere action of water, running over them as a stream or falling on them in drops; and he cites the Latin adage Gutta cavat lapidem non vi sed saepe cadendo — "constant droppings will make a hole in a flint" — and the like Greek proverb, that from frequent dropping, perpetually falling, even a stone is hollowed into a hole. The second clause, "thou washest away the things which grow out of the dust of the earth," Clarke refers to sudden falls of rain occasioning floods, by which the fruits of the earth are swept off; "and thus the hope of man — the grain for his household and the provender for his cattle — is destroyed."

The witnesses do not divide, and the two of them together let the verse work by its very quietness. It is not the earthquake or the landslide now but the drop of water, the slow overflow, the thing so small it seems no threat — and yet it is precisely this that hollows the flint and carries off the soil and the harvest. That, on their reading, is the terror Job means: not that some sudden catastrophe destroys a man, but that the ceaseless, patient pressure of affliction wears even the strongest away as surely as dripping water bores through stone, and washes off his hope as a flood washes off the standing corn. The gentleness of the image is its point, for what cannot be resisted by force is undone, in the end, by mere persistence.
20:
The wearing-down of nature passes into the plain statement of God's mastery over man: "thou prevailest for ever against him, and he passeth: thou changest his countenance, and sendest him away." The reformed John Gill reads the prevailing as absolute and final. God is more than a match for man in everything; there is no contending with him nor standing against him; no disease can be resisted when he sends it, for it is his messenger and does what he bids, and death itself "reigns with a despotic power, irresistibly, victoriously, and triumphantly," over all men in all ages. And this prevailing is "for ever," since the grave is man's long home from which he never returns to this world.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the disputed verb, taking it not as "thou provest thyself stronger than he" but in its transitive force of seizing and grasping — God "seizeth him for ever, then he passeth away; thou changest his countenance and castest him forth." The many sufferings God inflicts across a life are not what is meant; it is the one final overpowering of death. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws out the picture in the two remaining clauses. "It is impossible for him to withstand thee: every stroke of thine brings him down." And "thou changest his countenance" he takes as "probably an allusion to the custom of covering the face when the person was condemned, and sending him away to execution," as in the case of Haman, whose face they covered at Esth. 7:8.

John Wesley reads the whole with a mournful brevity: "when once thou takest away this life, it is gone for ever," and God "sendest him away — to his long home." The witnesses do not divide; they read one grim truth from three angles. Man is no match for God, and the contest is never for a moment in doubt: the stroke falls, the countenance is altered — whether by the disfigurement of death itself or, on Clarke's reading, by the covered face of the condemned led out to die — and the man is dismissed from the world, sent away to a home from which there is no coming back. It is the same finality the whole chapter has pressed, now stated as the sheer disproportion between the Almighty who prevails and the mortal who simply passes; and the tenderness Job had reached for in his hope of being remembered is, for the moment, swallowed up in the picture of a God against whom no man can stand.
21:
Job follows the dead man past his own end to the fortunes of his children, which can no longer touch him: "his sons come to honour, and he knoweth it not; and they are brought low, but he perceiveth it not of them." The reformed John Gill glosses the first clause — the sons "come to honour," or are multiplied, their families increasing like a flock; or "become heavy," loaded with gold and silver, raised to grandeur and dignity, possessed of much wealth and large estates — the very kind of blessing a living father most rejoices in, and of which the dead man knows nothing at all.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke states the point with unsparing plainness: when a man is dead "he is equally indifferent and unconscious whether his children have met with a splendid or oppressive lot in life; for as to this world, when man dies, in that day all his thoughts perish." Honour or ruin, the rise of his house or its fall, are alike beyond his knowing. John Wesley allows the words two senses that come to nearly the same thing — either the dead man "is ignorant of all such events," or he "is not concerned or affected with them" — and sums it in a line: "a dead or dying man minds not these things." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch simply carry the couplet forward with its companion, joining the sons who come to honour and are brought low to the flesh that has pain and the soul that mourns, as the chapter draws to its close.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, expounding the passage, draws from it a lesson in the moderating of our cares. When a man is in the hands of death's harbingers, tell him the most agreeable or the most painful news concerning his children, and it is all alike, for "he is going to that world where he will be a perfect stranger to all those things which here filled and affected him." The consideration of this, Henry says, should moderate our cares concerning our families: since God will know what becomes of our children when we are gone, to him let us commit them, and not burden ourselves with needless, fruitless anxieties about a future we shall not see. So the witnesses read the verse as one more stroke in Job's portrait of death's completeness — the world he loved going on without him, the standing of his sons wholly hidden from the one they most concerned — and turn the dead father's ignorance into a quiet argument for casting the weight of tomorrow upon the God who alone survives to watch it.
22:
The chapter ends on a note of solitary pain: "but his flesh upon him shall have pain, and his soul within him shall mourn." The reformed John Gill offers two constructions. The words may describe the dying man, chastened with strong pains on his sick and dying bed — which is why he neither rejoices in his family's honour nor grieves at their fall, having pain enough of his own to bear; or, with Aben Ezra and the Targum, they may describe the dead man in the grave, his flesh melting and corrupting where it lies, and his soul mourning over the body it once enlivened. Gill leans to reading the verse of the state of the dead, a continuation of the description of death itself.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sums the whole discourse in it: "the sum of the life of man is this, pain of body and distress of soul; and he is seldom without the one or the other, and often oppressed by both." But he lingers over how strangely the last verse has been rendered, and here a real difference of reading opens. Mr. Good turns it, "for his flesh shall drop away from him, and his soul shall become a waste from him"; the Chaldee, "his flesh, on account of the worms, shall grieve over him, and his soul, in the house of judgment, shall wail over him"; and Stock, whom Clarke thinks the most natural of all, "but over him his flesh shall grieve, and over him his breath shall mourn" — for "in the daring spirit of oriental poetry, the flesh and the breath are made conscious beings, the former lamenting its putrefaction in the grave, the latter mourning over the mouldering clay it once enlivened."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps the verse with the dying man and draws from it a warning. Reading "while his flesh is upon him... it shall have pain, and while his soul is within him... it shall mourn," he finds that "dying work is hard work, and dying pangs are commonly sore pangs"; it is folly, therefore, to defer repentance to a death-bed and leave the one thing needful to be done when a man is least fit to do anything, and true wisdom to treasure up beforehand the comforts that will relieve a dying hour. So the witnesses close the chapter on a genuine division of rendering — whether the pain and mourning belong to the man as he dies, as Henry and one side of Gill take it, or to his very flesh and soul in the grave, personified as conscious mourners over his own corruption, as the versions Clarke prefers would have it. Either way, the last word of Job's long meditation on mortality is one of unrelieved sorrow, body and soul alike given over to pain — the darkness out of which, in the chapters to come, his hope will have to climb again.
